analysis.one_liner: Would automatically repeal the Affordable Care Act if the number of uninsured Americans ever rose above its starting level.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to eight House committees and three subcommittees and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the Affordable Care Act and the health provisions of its 2010 companion law automatically, if a Government Accountability Office study ever found more uninsured Americans than existed before the ACA took effect [S2][S3]. Even if the law reduced the number of uninsured, the bill would claw back unobligated federal money for enrollment assistance, state exchanges, and implementation in proportion to the improvement, canceling it for debt reduction [S2][S3]. The bill proposed no replacement coverage.
analysis.who_benefits: If repeal triggered, high-income households would gain because the ACA's wholesale repeal includes its tax provisions, and drug and device makers would be freed of ACA fees; employers and insurers would shed the coverage mandates [S2][S3]. Even if the law kept reducing the uninsured count, the clawback would cut unobligated implementation money — consumer assistance, exchange grants, and the implementation fund — which proponents framed as debt reduction [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeal of the ACA and the 2010 companion law would erase the ACA's tax and fee provisions, including those borne by high earners, drug makers, and device makers, with no replacement revenue in the bill.
The automatic trigger means repeal would happen by GAO measurement rather than by a separate vote, removing congressional judgment from the decision once the bill passed.

The clawback rescinds unobligated funding for consumer assistance, state exchange establishment, and the Health Insurance Reform Implementation Fund in proportion to any drop in the uninsured count, canceling the money for debt reduction.

analysis.who_pays: People who gained coverage and protections under the ACA would bear the cost if repeal triggered: those with pre-existing conditions, young adults on parents' plans, Medicaid expansion enrollees, and the newly insured, all losing coverage with no substitute in the bill [S2][S3]. Even short of repeal, navigator and exchange programs would lose unobligated funding, and the Comptroller General would conduct a new study every 60 days for up to five years [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: If the uninsured count ever rose above its pre-ACA level, the entire law would vanish automatically — including protections for pre-existing conditions, young-adult coverage, the Medicaid expansion, and marketplace subsidies — with nothing replacing them, because the bill contains no replacement coverage provisions.

The clawback punishes the law's success: the more the uninsured count fell, the more unobligated money for enrollment help and state exchanges would be rescinded, potentially hobbling the very outreach that produced the improvement.

Requiring a Comptroller General study every 60 days for up to five years would impose a recurring measurement burden and tie health policy to statistical timing, since a temporary uptick in the uninsured count would trigger full repeal at that moment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered concentrated interests — high earners, drug and device makers — lower taxes and fees, but asked people who gained coverage under the ACA to give it up with no replacement, and set up a mechanism in which the law's implementation funding shrank in proportion to its success. Even a supporter would have to acknowledge that an automatic repeal trigger keyed to a headcount, with no transition plan or substitute coverage, made the coverage loss abrupt and unconditional.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to eight House committees and then to three subcommittees, and it sat there without a hearing, a vote, or floor action until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) introduced the Health Insurance Accountability Act of 2014 on January 10, 2014.
The same day it was referred to eight committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, Rules, and Appropriations.

It was then referred to subcommittees: Indian and Alaska Native Affairs on January 14, the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on January 17, and the Education and Workforce Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee on June 13, 2014.
No hearing, markup, or vote followed; the bill drew zero cosponsors and the last action of record was the June 2014 subcommittee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who hold or rely on ACA coverage and protections are better off, since the law stayed in place. No industry or interest gained anything from the outcome; the bill simply lapsed with no support beyond its sponsor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People holding ACA coverage and protections

for.name: Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill; it attracted no cosponsors from either party.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 17, 2014 and took no further recorded action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no party ever went on record for or against it beyond the sponsor's introduction.

industries.note: Repeal would free insurers of ACA coverage rules but also strip them of the subsidized marketplace customers and mandate-driven enrollment the law created; insurers generally sought to keep the law's subsidies and coverage requirements, so full repeal cut against their enrollment base. The clawback would also cut unobligated exchange-establishment funding.

Wholesale repeal of the ACA includes its tax provisions, so the highest earners would keep income now paid in additional Medicare taxes. That gain comes as lost revenue while millions would lose coverage or protections.
Repeal ends the ACA's annual fee on branded prescription drugs but also shrinks the insured market created by the coverage expansion. The fee relief is a direct gain at public cost.
Repeal removes the ACA's excise tax on device sales, a direct gain for the industry, financed by repealing the coverage measures that fund coverage for ordinary people.

Repeal would restore Medicare payments to hospitals serving many uninsured patients that the ACA cut, but would also raise uncompensated care as more people lost coverage. Hospitals would lose newly insured patients either way.
